params.question: A 50-year-old presents to the emergency department with a red left eye, severe pain, and sees halos around lights. The pupil is mid-dilated and fixed. Using the PPPCC danger signs, what is the appropriate immediate action?

answers.text: Prescribe topical antibiotic drops and review in 48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This patient has at least three PPPCC danger signs — Pain, Pupil abnormality (mid-dilated, fixed), and vision Change (seeing halos). Any single positive sign mandates urgent referral, not outpatient antibiotic treatment.

answers.text: Instil lubricant drops and advise warm compresses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Lubricants and warm compresses are appropriate for simple conjunctivitis with no danger signs. This patient has pain, a fixed dilated pupil, and visual symptoms — likely acute angle-closure glaucoma requiring emergency treatment.

answers.text: Refer urgently to ophthalmology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This patient has multiple PPPCC danger signs: Pain, Pupil abnormality (mid-dilated and fixed), and vision Change (halos). The presentation is consistent with acute angle-closure glaucoma. Any single PPPCC sign warrants urgent ophthalmology referral; three together make it an emergency.

answers.text: Start topical steroid drops and arrange outpatient follow-up

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical steroids without specialist assessment risk masking a sight-threatening diagnosis. With a fixed mid-dilated pupil and pain, this is likely angle-closure glaucoma, not an inflammatory condition suitable for empirical steroid therapy.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the PPPCC framework: Pain, Photophobia, Pupil abnormality, vision Change, and Corneal opacity or Ciliary flush. Any one positive sign means urgent referral.
Well done. Recognising danger signs and acting on even a single positive is the key skill in red-eye triage.

interactions.label: Four children in a school outbreak have red eyes with watery discharge and folli

params.question: Four children in a school outbreak have red eyes with watery discharge and follicular reactions on upper lid eversion. Two have fever and sore throat. A tender preauricular lymph node is palpable in all four. Which treatment is most appropriate?

answers.text: Topical chloramphenicol for all four children

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical antibiotics are ineffective against viral conjunctivitis and promote antimicrobial resistance. The combination of watery discharge, follicles, and preauricular lymphadenopathy is classic adenoviral conjunctivitis.

answers.text: Oral azithromycin for the two with fever only

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral azithromycin targets bacterial and chlamydial infections. The two children with fever and pharyngitis likely have pharyngoconjunctival fever (adenoviral), which resolves with supportive care.

answers.text: Supportive care for all four, with hand hygiene and infection control

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Watery discharge, follicular reaction, and tender preauricular nodes indicate adenoviral conjunctivitis. The two with fever and pharyngitis have pharyngoconjunctival fever. All four need supportive care only — lubricants and cold compresses. Emphasise strict hand hygiene, separate towels, and school exclusion to limit the outbreak. Warn about possible subepithelial infiltrates around day 14 in epidemic keratoconjunctivitis.

answers.text: Topical aciclovir for the two with fever

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Topical aciclovir is used for herpes simplex keratitis, not adenoviral conjunctivitis. Adenovirus has no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the viral conjunctivitis triad: watery discharge, follicular reaction, tender preauricular node. No antibiotics — supportive care only.
Exactly. The mnemonic 'F for Follicle, F for Viral' helps — follicles plus a preauricular node point to adenovirus, and antibiotics offer no benefit.

params.question: A community screening in a trachoma-endemic area finds that twelve percent of children aged one to nine have active trachoma (TF/TI). Several adults have trichiasis with lashes abrading the cornea. Which combination of SAFE strategy components should be implemented first?

answers.text: Antibiotics for symptomatic children and facial cleanliness education

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: With prevalence exceeding ten percent, mass antibiotic treatment of the entire community is indicated, not just symptomatic cases. Additionally, adults with trichiasis need urgent surgery — each blink deepens corneal damage, and antibiotics cannot reverse established scarring.

answers.text: Surgery for adults with trichiasis and mass antibiotic distribution for the community

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Adults with trichiasis need immediate bilamellar tarsal rotation to prevent further corneal damage, as antibiotics cannot reverse established scarring. With prevalence above ten percent in children, mass oral azithromycin is given to the entire community to interrupt transmission. Facial cleanliness and environmental improvements follow as sustained long-term interventions.

answers.text: Environmental improvement through latrine construction and clean water supply

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Environmental measures are essential for long-term control of the Musca sorbens vector but do not address the immediate threats: ongoing corneal damage from trichiasis in adults and active infection in children.

answers.text: Mass antibiotic distribution alone, with surgery deferred until scarring stabilises

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deferring surgery is dangerous. Each blink drives trichiatic lashes further into the cornea, causing progressive damage. Antibiotics clear active infection but cannot reverse cicatricial entropion — surgery must not be delayed.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the SAFE strategy: Surgery (bilamellar tarsal rotation for trichiasis), Antibiotics (mass azithromycin when prevalence >10%), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement. Prioritise S and A first.
Well done. In SAFE, Surgery and Antibiotics address the urgent threats; Facial cleanliness and Environmental improvement sustain long-term control.

params.question: An eight-year-old boy with known vernal keratoconjunctivitis develops a superficial oval corneal erosion during a seasonal flare. His mother reports he frequently rubs his eyes. What is the most likely cause of this corneal lesion?

answers.text: Secondary bacterial keratitis from contaminated hands

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While secondary infection can occur, the characteristic superficial oval erosion in VKC is a shield ulcer caused by eosinophil toxicity, not bacterial infection. Treating it as bacterial keratitis with aggressive antibiotics risks unnecessary scarring.

answers.text: Corneal abrasion from mechanical rubbing alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rubbing worsens VKC by releasing more histamine and can traumatise the cornea, but the characteristic oval erosion pattern is a shield ulcer — a specific complication of eosinophil-mediated epithelial damage, not simple mechanical injury.

answers.text: Eosinophil-mediated epithelial toxicity causing a shield ulcer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The shield ulcer is the sight-threatening complication of VKC. Eosinophils in the conjunctival tissue release toxic granule proteins that damage the corneal epithelium, producing a characteristic superficial oval erosion. It is not infective. Counsel patients never to rub — rubbing releases more histamine and worsens epithelial damage. Cold compresses are the safe alternative.

answers.text: Herpes simplex dendritic ulcer reactivated by seasonal allergens

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Herpes simplex produces a branching dendritic pattern with terminal bulbs, quite different from the oval shield ulcer of VKC. The clinical context of established VKC with a seasonal flare points squarely to eosinophil-mediated damage.

overallFeedback.feedback: In VKC, the shield ulcer is caused by eosinophil toxicity to the corneal epithelium, not infection. Recognising this prevents mismanagement as bacterial keratitis.
Correct. The shield ulcer is eosinophil-driven, not infective — and the no-rubbing rule is essential counselling for every VKC patient.

params.question: A 60-year-old glaucoma patient on topical timolol reports episodes of wheezing since starting the medication. Which modification to the instillation technique is most likely to reduce these systemic side-effects?

answers.text: Instilling two drops instead of one to ensure adequate intraocular dosing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Two drops would worsen systemic absorption. The conjunctival sac holds only 7–10 microlitres; a single drop (30–50 microlitres) already exceeds capacity. A second drop simply increases overflow and nasolacrimal drainage into the systemic circulation.

answers.text: Applying the drop directly onto the cornea for faster ocular absorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dropping onto the cornea causes discomfort and triggers a reflex blink that expels the medication. The drop should be instilled into the lower fornix pocket formed by gently pulling down the lower lid.

answers.text: Pressing the medial canthus for one to two minutes after instillation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Nasolacrimal occlusion — pressing the inner corner of the eye for 1–2 minutes — blocks drainage through the nasolacrimal duct. Without this step, excess timolol bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism and enters the systemic circulation directly from the nasal mucosa, causing beta-blocker effects such as bronchospasm. This simple technique significantly reduces systemic absorption.

answers.text: Keeping the eye wide open for thirty seconds after instillation to maximise corneal contact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Keeping the eye open increases evaporation and does not prevent nasolacrimal drainage. After instillation, the patient should close the eye gently without squeezing while performing nasolacrimal occlusion.

overallFeedback.feedback: The conjunctival sac holds only 7–10 µL, but a drop delivers 30–50 µL. The excess drains via the nasolacrimal duct into the bloodstream. Pressing the medial canthus for 1–2 minutes blocks this drainage.
Exactly. Nasolacrimal occlusion is the single most effective technique for reducing systemic absorption of topical ophthalmic drugs.
